nameStory: Trailing arbutus gets its name from its habit of trailing along the ground like a natural carpet. The name 'mayflower' comes from its sweet-scented pink and white flowers that bloom in early spring, around May. It's also called ground laurel because its evergreen leaves stay close to the forest floor year-round.
description: Trailing arbutus is a low-growing, woody shrub that hugs the ground and spreads by trailing stems. It rarely grows more than 6 inches tall but can spread several feet wide, forming dense mats. The plant has leathery, oval evergreen leaves and produces clusters of small, fragrant pink or white flowers in early spring. This member of the heath family is one of New England's earliest wildflowers to bloom.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats that hug the ground with trailing woody stems that root as they creep along

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Thick, leathery oval leaves that feel waxy and remain green all winter, with visible veins and slightly fuzzy undersides

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Clusters of small tubular flowers with 5 petals, ranging from pure white to deep pink, with an incredibly sweet fragrance that carries on warm spring days

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Woody, reddish-brown trailing stems that feel rough and are covered with rust-colored bristly hairs

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Small, round capsules that split open to reveal tiny seeds, though fruit production is often sparse

habitat: Found in acidic, well-drained sandy or rocky soils under pine and oak forests throughout New England. Prefers partially shaded areas with good drainage, often growing on slopes, in pine barrens, or along woodland edges. Commonly associated with blueberries, wintergreen, and other heath family plants in acidic forest conditions.

seasonality.spring: Produces its famous fragrant pink and white flowers from March through May, making it one of the earliest spring bloomers. The sweet scent is most noticeable on warm, sunny days.
seasonality.summer: Flowers fade and small capsule fruits may develop, though the plant often reproduces more by spreading stems than seeds. Leaves remain green and leathery.
seasonality.fall: Evergreen leaves may take on slight reddish tints in cold weather, and the trailing stems continue to spread and root.
seasonality.winter: Stays green under snow cover, with thick waxy leaves helping it survive freezing temperatures. The woody trailing stems and leaf arrangement are still visible for identification.

funFact: Trailing arbutus was so beloved that it became the official state flower of Massachusetts, and the Pilgrims named their ship the Mayflower after this plant - it was reportedly the first flower they saw blooming after their harsh first winter in the New World.
confusionNotes: Most often confused with wintergreen, but trailing arbutus has oval leaves (not round) and grows in trailing mats rather than upright. Unlike wintergreen, trailing arbutus leaves don't smell minty when crushed and the flowers are clustered rather than solitary.
contextualKnowledge: This plant is often called 'mayflower' in New England, but don't confuse it with the Canada mayflower (wild lily-of-the-valley) which is completely unrelated. Trailing arbutus has become quite rare in many areas due to habitat loss and over-picking, so it's protected in several states - look but don't pick!
compareHints: Trailing arbutus is the only species in its genus found in New England, making it unique among our flora. Compared to other heath family members like wintergreen or partridgeberry, it's distinguished by its distinctly trailing woody growth habit and clusters of tubular flowers. Most other low-growing heath plants either grow upright or have different leaf shapes and flower arrangements.
